passages.title: Pixel Learns to Shake
sentences: Sam wanted Pixel to learn to shake.
He held out his hand.
"Shake," he said.
Pixel just sat and looked at him.
Sam tried every day for a week.
On Sunday, Pixel lifted his paw.
He put it in Sam's hand.
Sam laughed and gave him a treat.
"Good boy!" he said. "We did it!"

passages.title: The Long Climb
sentences: Maya and her dad hiked the trail to the lookout on Lantern Peaks.
The trail was steep and rocky.
After an hour, Maya's legs felt heavy, and she wanted to stop.
"Let's rest for five minutes," said her dad.
They sat on a log and drank some water.
Then Maya stood up and kept going, one step at a time.
At last, they reached the top.
Maya could see the whole island below.
She saw the harbor, the ferry and the roof of her school.
The sea was blue all the way to the sky.
Maya took a deep breath and grinned.
"I climbed all of it," she said.

passages.title: Leo Helps Jai
sentences: A new boy named Jai came to the skate park with a brand new board.
He stepped on it, and the board rolled away without him.
Jai sat on the ground and looked at the board.
Leo rolled over and stopped next to him.
"That happened to me a lot when I started," Leo said.
"Put your front foot here, over the bolts."
"Bend your knees a little, like this."
Jai tried again, and this time he rolled a few feet.
Leo clapped.
"You'll get it," he said. "I'll be here on Saturday too."

passages.title: Ben's First Club Day
sentences: Ben stood outside Room 12 at Harbor Middle School.
It was the first day of robot club, and every face inside was new to him.
His hands were sweaty, and he thought about going home.
Then the door opened, and Priya waved him in.
"We need someone to build the arm," she said. "Want to try?"
She showed him the box of parts and the plan.
At first, Ben's fingers felt clumsy with the tiny screws.
Priya showed him how to use the small screwdriver.
By the end of the hour, the arm could lift a pencil.
Ben and Priya cheered when it worked.
On the way out, Ben asked, "Same time next week?"
Priya nodded. "Same time next week."

passages.title: Sam's Best Saturday
sentences: Sam's favorite kind of Saturday starts early.
He and Grandma Rose take the 8:15 AM train along the coast.
Sam sits by the window with his map and marks each station they pass.
Pixel rides on the floor by his feet.
At the last stop, they walk to the harbor to watch the big boats come in.
Grandma Rose brings two warm rolls from the bakery in a paper bag.
They eat them on a bench by the water.
Sam tells her facts about the trains, and she listens to every one.
On the ride home, Sam counts the bridges.
There are seven of them.
When they get back, Sam feels tired and happy at the same time.
"Same trip next month?" Grandma Rose asks.
Sam nods fast.

passages.title: Camping in the Living Room
sentences: Ana and Ben had a plan for Saturday.
They would camp with their mom at the Story Woods campsite.
Ben had packed his sleeping bag, a flashlight and a deck of cards three days early.
On Friday night, the weather report showed a big storm coming to the island.
There would be strong wind and heavy rain all weekend.
"I'm sorry," said Mom. "It is not safe to camp in a storm like that."
Ben dropped his bag on the floor and frowned.
Ana felt disappointed too, but then she had an idea.
"What if we camp in the living room?" she asked.
Mom smiled and helped them set up the tent between the couch and the window.
That night, the wind was loud, and the rain hit the glass.
Inside the tent, the twins played cards by flashlight and ate popcorn.
Before he fell asleep, Ben said, "This is a pretty good camping trip."
"We can go to Story Woods next month," Mom said. "The campsite will still be there."

passages.title: Leo Keeps the Beat
sentences: For his birthday, Leo got a practice pad and a new pair of drumsticks.
A practice pad is a flat rubber circle that drummers hit to train their hands.
It makes a soft tap instead of a loud bang, so his family did not mind the noise.
Leo already played the drums in the Grade 7 band, but the band's newest song had a hard new part for him.
In the middle of the song, he had to play a steady beat alone for one whole minute without speeding up.
The first week was harder than he expected.
Every time Leo got excited, his hands moved faster, and the beat got quicker and quicker.
He felt frustrated, and twice he put the sticks away in a drawer.
Then the band teacher showed him a metronome app on her tablet.
A metronome clicks at an even speed, and a drummer plays one hit on each click.
"Start slow," she told him. "Practice for fifteen minutes every day, and only speed up when slow feels easy."
Leo took the sticks out of the drawer and followed her plan, even on days when he wanted to be at the skate park.
He counted out loud, one, two, three, four, and waited for each click before he hit the pad.
After six weeks, he played the part for the band teacher again.
The beat stayed steady for the whole minute, and she nodded.
"That part is ready for the concert," she said.
Leo grinned and tapped his sticks together twice.

passages.title: Ana's Chess Match
sentences: On Monday afternoons, the Harbor Town library holds a chess club in its back room.
Ana had played chess with her brother Ben for a year, and she won most of their games.
So when Maya asked her to play, Ana felt sure that she would win.
Twenty minutes later, Maya slid her queen across the board and said quietly, "Checkmate."
Ana stared at the board in silence.
Her king was completely trapped, with no safe square left to move to.
On the walk home, Ana told Ben that she did not want to go back to chess club.
Ben thought about it for a moment. "You could ask Maya to explain how she beat you," he suggested.
The next Monday, Ana walked up to Maya's table and asked.
Maya set up the pieces again and showed her the moves that had trapped her king.
"You brought your queen out too early," Maya explained. "I did that for months when I started."
After that, Ana practiced on a chess app for twenty minutes after her homework.
She solved one puzzle each day and wrote every new idea in a small notebook.
A month later, she and Maya played again.
This time, the game lasted almost an hour, and it ended in a draw, with neither player able to win.
Ana and Maya shook hands, and both of them laughed.
"Rematch next Monday?" asked Maya, and Ana said yes.

passages.title: Maya's Triceratops
sentences: When Maya opened the box from her aunt, she found a model kit of a Triceratops skeleton.
Inside were 214 plastic bones, a tube of glue, a wooden stand and a thick booklet of instructions.
Triceratops was a plant-eating dinosaur that lived about 68 to 66 million years ago, in what is now western North America.
Its name means "three-horned face," because it had two long horns above its eyes and a shorter one on its nose.
Maya planned to build one section every weekend and to finish in six weeks, in time for the school science fair.
The first two weekends went smoothly.
She sorted the bones into labeled cups, then glued together the long tail and the four thick legs.
On the third weekend, she reached the skull, which the booklet called the hardest part of the kit.
The wide frill at the back of the skull was made of five thin pieces that had to line up exactly.
As she pressed the last piece into place, the frill cracked down the middle.
Maya set it down, pushed back her chair and did not touch the model for the rest of the day.
The next morning, she studied the crack more carefully.
She remembered from a library book that real fossil bones are often found broken into many pieces.
Scientists clean each piece, fit the pieces back together and glue them, one careful step at a time.
So Maya did the same thing: she lined up the two halves, added a thin line of glue and held them still for five whole minutes.
When the glue dried, the crack was a fine line that people could only see up close.
She decided not to paint over it.
Maya attached the last rib on the Friday before the fair.
At her table, she set the model next to a card that said, "Built in six weeks. One crack, fixed the way scientists fix real fossils."
Many visitors asked about the crack, and Maya explained how fossils are repaired.
Ms. Ortiz looked at the frill for a long time.
"The crack is my favorite part," she said.

passages.title: Learning to Live in Space
sentences: On the International Space Station, everyday activities like sleeping, eating and exercising work very differently than they do at home.
The station circles Earth about once every 90 minutes, so the crew can see about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets in a single day.
Most astronauts stay on board for about six months, which means they must learn a whole new set of daily routines.
Sleeping is one of the first routines that changes.
Because everything floats, astronauts zip themselves into sleeping bags that are tied to the wall of a small cabin, about the size of a closet.
In space there is no real up or down, so sleeping sideways feels the same as sleeping upright.
Eating changes too.
Drinks come in pouches with straws, because water poured from a cup would float away in wobbly drops.
Crews often eat tortillas instead of bread, since bread makes crumbs that drift around the station and can get into machines.
Staying healthy takes daily work.
Without gravity pulling on their bodies, astronauts' bones and muscles slowly become weaker.
To stay strong, they exercise for about two hours every day on a treadmill, an exercise bike and a lifting machine, using straps to hold themselves in place.
Astronauts often say that their first few days on the station feel strange and clumsy.
They bump into walls, let go of pencils that float away, and forget to strap things down.
Little by little, though, the new routines start to feel normal.
When they return to Earth months later, they have to get used to gravity again, and walking can feel wobbly for a while.
Learning a new routine takes time and patience, whether you are in space or at home.

passages.title: Maya's Shiny Rock
sentences: On Saturday, Maya walked along the creek in Story Woods.
She was looking for rocks for her shelf.
Near the water, she found a gray rock with shiny gold cubes.
"Is this real gold?" she wondered.
On Tuesday, she took it to rock club.
Mr. Varga looked at it with a hand lens.
"This is pyrite," he said. "It looks like gold, but it is a different mineral."
"Pyrite often grows in tiny cubes like these."
Maya looked at the cubes again.
They had flat sides and sharp corners.
She liked them even more now.
At home, she put the rock on her shelf with a new label: "Pyrite, Story Woods creek."
Then she stood back and smiled.

passages.title: Too Loud at the Game Fair
sentences: Ben and Ana went to the Harbor Town Game Fair.
Inside the big tent, it was very loud.
Games beeped, music played, and people shouted.
Ben covered his ears with his hands.
The noise made it hard for him to think.
Ana looked at him. "Do you want a break?" she asked.
Ben nodded.
They got hand stamps at the gate and went outside to a quiet bench by the harbor.
Ben put on his headphones and drank some water.
After ten minutes, he felt calm again.
"Okay," he said. "Now I want to try the racing game."
He kept his headphones on and played three races.
In the last race, he came in second.

credit.title: Too Loud at the Game Fair
credit.author: Learning to Fly (AI-drafted)

passages.title: The Wild Boar and the Fox
sentences: One calm afternoon, a wild boar stood next to an old oak tree in the forest.
A wild boar is a kind of wild pig with two long, sharp teeth called tusks.
The boar rubbed his tusks against the bark, again and again, to make them sharper.
A fox walked by and stopped to watch.
"Why are you doing that?" the fox asked.
"The forest is quiet today, and there is no danger anywhere."
The boar did not stop.
"That is exactly why I am doing it now," he said.
"If danger comes, I will have to move fast."
"There will be no time to sharpen my tusks then."
"So I get ready today, while everything is calm."
The fox thought carefully about this answer on his long walk home.
He decided that the boar was wiser than he had expected.
The best time to get ready is before you need to be ready.

credit.title: The Wild Boar and the Fox
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Travelers and the Sea
sentences: Two travelers were walking along the seashore on a bright, windy afternoon.
Far out on the water, they saw something dark floating on the waves.
"Look!" said the first traveler. "That must be a big ship coming to the harbor."
They were excited, so they sat down on the sand to watch it arrive.
Slowly, the wind and the waves pushed the dark shape closer to the shore.
"It is smaller than I thought," said the second traveler. "Maybe it is only a little boat."
They waited a little longer.
At last, a wave carried the thing right up onto the beach.
It was not a ship, and it was not a boat.
It was only a bundle of sticks tied together with a rope.
The two travelers looked at each other and laughed.
Then they brushed the sand off their clothes and walked on.
Things that are far away can seem bigger than they really are.

credit.title: The Travelers and the Sea
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Practice at Seven
sentences: In July, a heat wave came to Harbor Town.
For a whole week, the afternoons were hotter than 95 degrees.
Coach Novak sent a message to the soccer team.
"It is not safe to run hard in this heat," the message said.
"This week, practice will start at 7:00 AM, before the day gets hot."
Ben read the message twice and groaned.
He liked to sleep late in the summer.
On Monday, his alarm rang at 6:15 AM, and the sky was still gray.
Ana and Ben rode their bikes to Pier Field, yawning the whole way.
But the air was cool, and the grass was wet and shiny.
Over the harbor, the sun was coming up, big and orange.
The team ran drills, and nobody felt too hot.
By Friday, Ben was waking up before his alarm.
"I like early practice more than I thought I would," he told Ana on the ride home.
"Me too," said Ana. "We get to see the sunrise."

passages.title: Priya's Rover Talk
sentences: Priya had built a small rover with four wheels and a camera on top.
Mrs. Hall asked her to show it at the library on Saturday.
Twenty people came, and most of them were younger kids.
Priya's heart beat fast when she saw all the faces.
She had written her talk on three cards, so she read the first card slowly.
Then she set the rover on the floor and pressed a button.
It rolled forward, saw a chair leg with its camera and turned left.
The kids gasped, and one girl clapped.
"How does it know where to go?" a boy asked.
Priya forgot about her cards.
She explained how the camera sends pictures to a tiny computer inside the rover.
The computer decides when to turn.
She answered questions for twenty minutes.
At the end, Mrs. Hall thanked her, and the kids lined up to watch the rover one more time.
Priya packed it up slowly, smiling the whole time.

passages.title: Leo Comes Over
sentences: On Sunday afternoon, Leo visited Sam's house for the first time.
The night before, Sam had cleaned his room and organized his shelves.
He also made a rule card for the model train layout in his room.
It said, "Look first. Ask before you touch."
When Leo arrived, Pixel raced to the front door and wagged his tail hard.
Sam showed Leo the layout on the big table next to his window.
It had two loops of track, a stone bridge, a tunnel and a tiny station.
Leo read the card and nodded. "Fair rule," he said.
He pointed at the freight train. "Can I drive that one?"
Sam showed him the controller and explained how to go slowly around the curve.
Then Leo showed Sam a video of his newest skateboard trick.
They shared a bowl of popcorn and ran both trains at the same time.
When Leo's dad came to pick him up, Leo said, "Next time, come to the skate park with me."
Sam said yes, and he meant it.

passages.title: Waiting for Launch Day
sentences: When a rocket is ready to launch, crowds often gather on beaches and roads nearby to watch.
Families bring chairs, snacks and binoculars, and some of them travel for hours to get there.
Yet many launches do not happen on the first day they are planned.
A launch that is called off for the day is known as a scrub.
Weather is one of the most common reasons for a scrub.
Strong winds high above the ground can push a rocket away from its planned path.
Some thick clouds carry electric charges, and a rocket flying through them could cause a lightning strike.
Engineers also watch readings from many sensors on the rocket, and if one reading looks wrong, they stop the countdown.
Each rocket also has a launch window, which is the period of time when it is able to leave.
Some launch windows last a few hours, but others last only a few seconds.
For the people watching, a scrub means more waiting.
Some families go home and return the next day, while others camp nearby.
Launch teams say that a scrub is a good decision, not a failure, because a safe launch matters more than a fast one.
When the rocket finally rises, many watchers say that the long wait made the moment even better.

passages.title: Sam's Map to the Bakery
sentences: For a social studies project, Mr. Lee asked each student to draw a map of a route they walk often.
Sam chose the walk from his house to Rose's Bakery, which he took with Pixel almost every Saturday.
He wanted his map to be accurate, so he decided to measure the distances himself.
On Saturday, he counted his steps between each corner while Pixel trotted beside him.
There were 212 steps from his front gate to the bus stop, and 340 more to the bakery door.
At home, Sam turned his steps into lines on graph paper, with one square for every ten steps.
He drew the streets in black, the bus stop as a blue circle and the bakery as a small brown square.
He added a key in the corner, so readers would know what each color and shape meant.
When Grandma Rose looked at the map, she smiled, but then she tapped the paper.
"My bakery is on the other side of Pine Street," she said gently.
Sam's face felt hot, because he had checked every number twice.
He had counted the steps correctly, but he had drawn the bakery on the wrong side of the street.
Sam did not start over.
He covered the square with a small piece of white paper and drew the bakery again, on the correct side.
On Monday, Mr. Lee hung the map on the classroom wall, and two classmates used it to plan a walk to the bakery.
Sam was proud of his map, and he was proud of the fix too.

passages.title: The Gold Pan
sentences: At the end of the rock club's tour of the Ridgeway Mine Museum, Mr. Varga led everyone to a long wooden trough full of muddy water.
"Today you can try gold panning," he said, and he handed each student a wide, shallow metal pan.
Maya scooped up a pan of sand and gravel.
She had read about panning in a library book, but she had never tried it.
On her first try, Maya shook the pan hard and tipped it quickly.
Water, sand and pebbles poured over the edge, and soon the pan was empty.
If there had been any gold inside, it was gone now.
Mr. Varga crouched beside her.
"Gold is very heavy," he explained. "A piece of gold weighs about nineteen times as much as the same amount of water."
"If you swirl the pan slowly, the gold sinks to the bottom, and the lighter sand washes away over the edge."
Maya tried again, and this time she moved slowly.
She swirled, tipped the pan a little, let the light sand wash out and then swirled again.
It took almost twenty minutes, and her arms began to ache.
At last, only a thin layer of black sand was left, and three tiny yellow flakes shone in it.
Mr. Varga helped her drop the flakes into a small glass tube of water.
They were smaller than grains of rice, but Maya held the tube up to the light and grinned.
On the bus home, she showed the tube to everyone in her row.

passages.title: Ben's Hardest Level
sentences: For three weeks, Ben designed and built a level in the game club's game-making app.
It was a castle full of moving platforms, falling blocks and long jumps over lava.
Ben tested every jump himself, and he was proud that his level was so difficult.
On Friday, he let Ana, Sam and Leo play it at the club.
Nobody got past the third jump.
Leo tried eleven times and then put the controller down.
"Is this even possible?" he asked.
Ben crossed his arms. "It is possible. I did it," he said, a little too loudly.
Then he watched Sam try, and he noticed something.
Sam pressed the jump button at exactly the right moment, but his character still fell into the lava every time.
Ben had practiced that jump for three weeks, so he knew a special trick that new players did not know.
That night, Ben made the third jump a little shorter.
He also added a checkpoint, so players who fell would not have to start the whole castle again.
The next Friday, Sam reached the end on his sixth try, and everyone at the table cheered.
Ben grinned.
He had learned that a level is more enjoyable when other players are able to finish it.

passages.title: A Song for Grandma Rose
sentences: Every morning, Grandma Rose hums the same old song while she shapes bread at the bakery.
For her birthday, Sam decided to learn the song on his guitar and play it for her.
He found the chords in a songbook at the library.
A chord is a group of notes played at the same time.
The song used only three chords, but one of them, called F, was hard for a new player.
To play it, Sam had to press his first finger across all six strings at once, and at first the strings buzzed.
Sam made a plan.
Every day after school, he practiced for twenty minutes, and he spent the first five minutes on the F chord alone.
He also practiced moving from one chord to the next very slowly, so that the moves would start to feel easy.
After two weeks, the buzz was gone, and after three weeks, he could play the whole song without stopping.
On her birthday, the family met at the bakery after it closed.
Sam sat on a stool between the tables and started to play.
His hands shook a little, and in the second verse, he missed the F chord.
He did not stop, and he went on to the next chord, the way he had practiced.
By the last verse, Grandma Rose was singing along, and her eyes were shiny.
"This is the best present I have ever had," she said, and she hugged him for a long time.

passages.title: Puppies in Training
sentences: A guide dog helps a person who is blind or has low vision to walk safely from place to place.
Guide dogs stop at curbs, lead their partners around things in the way and stay calm in busy places.
No puppy is born knowing how to do this.
Its training starts when it is about eight weeks old, and it takes around two years.
First, the puppy lives for about a year with a volunteer family, called puppy raisers.
The raisers teach it house manners, such as waiting at the door and staying off the furniture.
They also take the puppy almost everywhere they go, so it can get used to new places.
Wearing a small vest that says it is in training, the puppy rides buses, visits stores and lies quietly under café tables.
Each new place has new sounds and smells, and at first many puppies seem unsure.
Little by little, the strange places start to feel normal.
Next, the dog goes back to the guide dog school for several months of training with a professional trainer.
It learns to guide a person around obstacles and to stop at the edge of every curb and stair.
Not every dog finishes the program, and some move on to other jobs that suit them better.
The dogs that graduate are matched with a partner, and the two of them learn to work as a team.

passages.title: Ana in Goal
sentences: Ana usually played forward for her soccer team, because scoring goals was her favorite part of every game.
On Saturday, ten minutes before a game at Pier Field, Coach Novak called her over to the bench.
"Our regular goalkeeper is away visiting family this weekend," Coach Novak explained. "Would you be willing to play in goal today?"
Ana did not answer immediately.
She had never played goalkeeper in a real game, and she had been planning all week to score for her team.
Then she looked at her teammates, who were waiting for her answer, and she nodded.
Coach Novak handed her the heavy goalkeeper gloves and gave her three quick instructions.
"Keep your knees bent. Watch the ball, not the players. And call out loudly so your defenders always know where you are."
In the first half, a powerful shot flew past her fingertips into the net, and the other team celebrated.
Ana wiped her gloves on her shorts, took a slow breath and got into position again.
In the second half, she dove to her left and pushed a hard, low shot around the post.
Her teammates rushed over and patted her on the back.
The game ended in a tie, one goal to one.
Ana had not scored a single goal, but she had stopped four shots.
On the walk home, Ben asked her how it had felt to be the goalkeeper.
"Scary at first," Ana admitted. "But I liked being able to see the whole field. Maybe I will try it again."

passages.title: The Miller, His Son and the Donkey
sentences: Long ago, a miller and his young son decided to sell their donkey at the market in the next town.
A miller is a person who grinds grain into flour at a mill.
Hoping to keep the donkey rested and healthy for the sale, they walked beside it along the dusty country road.
Before long, they passed a group of travelers relaxing in the shade of an enormous chestnut tree.
"Look at those two," one traveler said with a laugh. "They have a perfectly good donkey, and they are walking!"
Embarrassed, the miller immediately lifted his son onto the donkey's back, and they continued on their journey.
Soon they met several elderly men who frowned disapprovingly at the boy.
"The young boy rides while his tired father walks," one of them said. "That is not right."
The boy climbed down, and the miller rode instead.
A little later, a group of women gathering water at a well pointed at them.
"How can that man ride comfortably while his small son struggles to keep up?" they asked.
So the miller pulled his son up beside him, and the donkey carried them both.
Near the entrance to the town, a shopkeeper called out to them from his doorway.
"That poor donkey is carrying far too much," he said. "You two are strong enough to carry it instead!"
The miller and his son climbed down, tied the donkey's legs to a long pole and lifted it onto their shoulders.
People on the bridge laughed at the strange sight, and the noise frightened the donkey.
It kicked so hard that the ropes came loose, and it splashed down into the shallow river.
The donkey scrambled out on the far bank and trotted away down the road, and the miller and his son could not catch it.
Disappointed and exhausted, the miller and his son walked home slowly, with no donkey and no money.
"We tried to please everyone," the miller said with a sigh, "and in the end we pleased nobody, not even ourselves."

credit.title: The Miller, His Son and the Donkey
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Counting Fish on the Reef
sentences: Scientists who study coral reefs cannot be everywhere at once, so many of them get help from trained volunteers.
The volunteers are people like students, teachers and grandparents who love the ocean.
Before they ever get wet, they spend weeks learning the names of dozens of kinds of reef fish from photos and cards.
They learn how to recognize a parrotfish or a wrasse by its shape, its colors and the way it swims.
On survey day, the volunteers snorkel or dive along a long measuring tape that has been laid across the reef.
This line is called a transect, and it makes sure that every survey covers the same area.
Each volunteer carries a white plastic slate and a pencil, because a pencil can still write underwater.
As they move slowly along the tape, they count certain kinds of fish that they see within a short distance of the line.
Moving slowly matters, because many fish hide when a swimmer rushes past.
Back on land, the volunteers type their counts into a computer.
Over many years, the numbers show scientists which fish are becoming more common and which are becoming rare.
These numbers help people decide which parts of a reef need to be protected.
Many volunteers say that their first survey was confusing, because the fish moved quickly and looked different underwater than in the photos.
Some of them counted the same fish twice or forgot to write a number down.
With practice, though, they learned to recognize each kind of fish quickly.
Several volunteers have said that learning the names of the fish made them notice far more on every swim than they had noticed before.

passages.title: Are Birds Dinosaurs?
sentences: For more than a hundred years, most people imagined dinosaurs as slow, scaly giants that had all died out long ago.
Today, most scientists think that one group of dinosaurs never completely disappeared.
They believe that birds, including the pigeons and gulls you see every day, are living dinosaurs.
The first clues came from bones.
In the 1860s, workers in a stone quarry in Germany found the fossil of an animal that seemed to be part bird and part reptile.
It had feathers and wings, but it also had teeth, claws on its wings and a long, bony tail.
Later, scientists noticed that birds and some small, meat-eating dinosaurs share many other features, such as hollow bones, a wishbone and three main toes that point forward.
Not everyone agreed at first.
For a long time, some scientists argued that these shared features were only a coincidence.
Then, starting in the 1990s, people digging in China found many dinosaur fossils with clear marks of feathers preserved in fine rock.
Some of these dinosaurs could not fly at all, which suggests that feathers first helped them stay warm or display colors to each other.
Faced with this new evidence, many scientists changed their minds.
Changing your mind can feel uncomfortable, especially when you have believed something for years.
But good scientists change their ideas when strong new evidence appears, and they explain clearly what made them change.
Because of that, what we know about dinosaurs keeps improving.
The next time a gull lands on the harbor railing, take a close look at its scaly feet and its three forward toes.
You may be looking at a dinosaur.

passages.title: Learning the Route
sentences: Before a train driver can carry passengers on a route alone, the driver must learn that route in great detail.
Railway workers call this route knowledge.
A driver needs to know every signal, every station, every curve and every hill along the line, sometimes across more than a hundred miles of track.
Drivers must know where the track goes up or down, because a heavy train needs a long distance to speed up or to slow down.
Learning a route takes weeks or even months.
New drivers ride in the cab beside an experienced driver, again and again, in daylight and in darkness.
They study track maps and write their own notes about each part of the line.
Many drivers draw simple diagrams that mark where to begin slowing down for each station.
On some railways, they also watch videos filmed from the front of a train, so they can see the route many times before they drive it.
At first, all the trees, bridges and signals can look the same.
Little by little, each place becomes familiar.
Drivers start to recognize a certain bridge as the sign that a curve is coming, or a certain tower as the place to begin braking.
Then an expert rides along to check that the driver truly knows the route before the driver may drive it alone.
Experienced drivers often say that, after many years, they can describe every part of their route from memory.
Knowing a route that well keeps passengers safe, and it also lets a driver notice right away when something is different, such as a new sign or a fallen branch.

passages.title: The Winter Bird Count
sentences: On a frosty Saturday in December, Sam and Maya volunteered for the annual winter bird count in Story Woods.
Every year, volunteers walk set paths through the woods and count every bird they see or hear, and the numbers go to scientists who study how bird populations change.
A guide from the nature center handed each of them a clipboard with a checklist of the local birds.
"At each stop, we stand completely still for ten minutes," she explained. "Birds hide when people move around or talk."
At the first stop, the ten minutes seemed incredibly long to Sam.
His toes were cold, and he kept checking the time on the guide's watch.
He could see nothing except bare branches against a gray, cloudy sky.
Maya leaned over and whispered, "Close your eyes and just listen."
Sam closed his eyes, and gradually he began to hear sounds that he had not noticed before.
There was a soft whistle from somewhere high up, a quick knocking on wood and a call that sounded like "chick-a-dee-dee-dee."
The guide smiled and nodded. "That last one is a black-capped chickadee. It calls its own name."
The knocking came from a downy woodpecker, which was tapping a dead branch to find insects hiding under the bark.
After that, Sam completely stopped looking at the guide's watch.
At the third stop, he heard a high, thin call before anyone else did, and he pointed up into a pine tree.
A tiny brown bird was creeping up the trunk in a spiral.
"Brown creeper," the guide whispered, and she let Sam write it on the checklist himself.
By noon, the group had recorded 63 individual birds of 14 different species.
On the way back to the parking lot, Sam walked more slowly than before, listening carefully.
"I always thought the woods were quiet in winter," he told Maya. "They are actually full of sounds."

passages.title: Sam Learns Table Tennis
sentences: The community center on Harbor Street had a table tennis table in the back room, and Ben played there whenever he had a free afternoon.
One afternoon in March, he asked Sam to play a game to eleven points.
Sam had never played before, but he liked the quick tapping sound of the ball on the table, so he agreed.
Ben won eleven to two.
Sam's two points came from Ben's mistakes, not from his own shots.
Sam did not enjoy losing, but he was also curious about why the ball kept flying off his paddle in unexpected directions.
Ben showed him how to hold the paddle loosely in a grip called the handshake grip, and how to keep his wrist steady instead of flicking it.
Then Ben gave him a goal: hit the ball back and forth over the net fifty times in a row, with no score, just for practice.
On the first day, Sam's best was seven.
He came back twice more that week, and at home he practiced bouncing a ball on his paddle while Pixel watched from the couch.
By the end of the second week, Sam and Ben reached fifty in a row, and they cheered so loudly that the community center's manager opened the door to check on them.
Three weeks after their first game, Sam asked for a rematch.
This time, he won six points with his own shots.
Ben still won the game, eleven to six, but the rallies were much longer, and the ball crossed the net many times during each point.
Afterward, Sam carefully wrote both scores, 2 and 6, on a sticky note and attached it inside his notebook.
"Next time, I want eight," he said.
Ben laughed and picked up the ball. "Then we should definitely keep practicing."

steps.say: First I find how Sam felt. He laughed and said, "We did it!" He felt proud.
Sam felt proud because he tried every day for a week, and then it worked.
Now I think about my own life. When did I try many times, and then it worked?
I remember when I learned something new. It took a lot of tries.
So I build: Like Sam, I felt proud when I learned something new. I tried many times. Your answer can be different. Any true answer is fine.
